reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant form of brittle bone disease caused by a recurrent mutation in the 5' untranslated region of IFITM5 (encoding BRIL), not by a collagen defect
Almost all cases share the same recurrent variant, creating a distinctive and highly consistent phenotype

Three characteristic features distinguish it: exuberant hyperplastic callus after fractures or surgery, calcification of the forearm interosseous membrane, and a dense radio-opaque metaphyseal band adjacent to the growth plate
Interosseous membrane calcification restricts forearm rotation, limiting pronation and supination
Sclerae are typically normal (not blue) and dentinogenesis imperfecta is absent, unlike classic collagen-related OI
Hyperplastic callus can be large, warm, and painful, mimicking osteosarcoma or infection and prompting unnecessary biopsy
Management mirrors other OI with fracture care, physiotherapy, and antiresorptive bisphosphonate therapy for skeletal fragility, while avoiding misdiagnosis of the exuberant callus
reference.pathophysiology: OI type V is caused by a recurrent point mutation in the 5' untranslated region of IFITM5, which creates a new upstream start codon and adds five amino acids to the BRIL protein expressed by osteoblasts. BRIL participates in bone mineralisation, and the mutant protein disturbs normal osteoblast function and matrix mineralisation, producing brittle bones without the type I collagen abnormality of classic OI. The altered bone biology manifests as an exaggerated reparative response, generating hyperplastic callus, and abnormal soft-tissue mineralisation such as calcification of the forearm interosseous membrane and a characteristic dense metaphyseal band. Bone histology shows a distinctive mesh-like (irregular) lamellar pattern. The result is increased fracture risk with these unique radiological and clinical hallmarks.
additionalDifferentials: Osteosarcoma or other bone tumour mimicked by hyperplastic callus
Non-accidental injury in a child with multiple fractures
Other rare non-collagen OI subtypes (e.g. SERPINF1-related)
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs demonstrating hyperplastic callus, interosseous membrane calcification, and the dense metaphyseal band
Assessment of forearm pronation and supination for restriction
Bone densitometry to quantify skeletal fragility
Examination of sclerae and dentition, characteristically normal in this subtype
Bone histology showing the irregular mesh-like lamellar pattern where biopsy is performed
Targeted IFITM5 mutation testing to confirm the recurrent variant
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging, warm, painful callus raising concern for malignancy or infection before OI type V is recognised
Fixed loss of forearm rotation from interosseous calcification
Spinal fractures or scoliosis compromising function
reference.prognosis: Skeletal fragility is lifelong but generally responsive to fracture management and antiresorptive therapy; forearm rotation may remain limited, and the main avoidable harm comes from misdiagnosing hyperplastic callus as tumour.
pitfalls: Biopsying or resecting hyperplastic callus mistaken for osteosarcoma, which can itself provoke more callus
Expecting blue sclerae or dentinogenesis imperfecta and discounting OI when they are absent
Overlooking the diagnostic triad of callus, interosseous calcification, and metaphyseal band on imaging
Failing to test IFITM5 because collagen gene studies are normal
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
management: Antiresorptive bisphosphonate therapy to reduce skeletal fragility and fracture frequency
Standard orthopaedic fracture management with awareness that fractures and surgery can provoke exuberant hyperplastic callus
Recognition of hyperplastic callus as a feature of the disease rather than osteosarcoma or infection, avoiding unnecessary biopsy, with anti-inflammatory analgesia for painful callus
Physiotherapy and occupational adaptation for restricted forearm pronation and supination from interosseous membrane calcification, with selective corrective surgery
Monitoring of bone mineral density and fracture pattern over time
Genetic counselling and confirmatory targeted testing for the recurrent autosomal dominant IFITM5 variant
Multidisciplinary metabolic bone and clinical genetics follow-up
